summary: Surveys IPv4 addressing dependencies in IETF Application Area standards-track and experimental documents, to help redesign them to be address independent or dual-stack. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A checklist of rules for apps that mention old-style addresses, so they can be updated.

questions: ipv4 dependencies in application area specs
subtitle: Surveying IPv4 dependencies in application layer standards

tldr.problem: As the internet transitions from IPv4 to IPv6, many application-layer standards have explicit dependencies on IPv4 addressing, making them unable to work correctly in an IPv6-only environment.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC systematically reviews all standards-track and experimental RFCs in the IETF Application Area, documenting which ones contain IPv4 dependencies and the specific places those dependencies appear.
tldr.outcome: The survey identifies standards that need updating to support IPv6 or become address-independent, providing a roadmap for the transition work that followed. Most dependencies were in protocols like FTP, HTTP, and DNS that later gained IPv6 support.

today: RFC 3795 is an Informational document published in June 2004. It catalogs IPv4 dependencies that existed at that time. Many of the standards it identified as dependent on IPv4 have since been updated or obsoleted by newer, IPv6-capable versions (such as RFC 3986 for URIs and RFC 3977 for NNTP). The survey itself has not been superseded but remains a historical record of transition challenges.

sections.title: The Challenge: Updating Applications for IPv6
sections.content:
The transition from IPv4 to IPv6 requires more than just updating network protocols; application-layer standards must also evolve. Many IETF standards documents for applications like FTP, HTTP, and email define how to handle IP addresses explicitly, often assuming only IPv4's four-byte dotted-decimal format (such as 192.0.2.1).

This RFC is one of seven documents (organized by IETF area) that catalogues all IPv4 dependencies in current standards. The goal is to identify which standards need redesign to be address-independent or at least to support both IPv4 and IPv6, providing a clear priority list for the transition effort.
sections.plainLanguage: Some internet rules were written with the old address format baked in. This document finds all those places in the application rules so people know what to update.

sections.title: What the Survey Covers
sections.content:
The survey covers standards-track RFCs (Full, Draft, and Proposed Standards) and Experimental RFCs in the IETF Application Area up to RFC 3200, with a few exceptions for later RFCs that obsolete earlier ones. RFCs are examined sequentially by number and classified by maturity level.

For each RFC, the document notes whether it contains IPv4 dependencies and where. A dependency might be a hardcoded port number used only with IPv4, a reference to the IPv4 address format, a protocol exchange that assumes dotted-decimal notation, or even an example that uses an IPv4 address.
sections.plainLanguage: The survey goes through the rulebook page by page, marking every spot where the rules mention "old-style addresses" and nothing else.

sections.title: Common IPv4 Dependencies
sections.content:
The survey finds that several well-known protocols have clear IPv4 dependencies. FTP (RFC 959) uses commands like PORT h1,h2,h3,h4,p1,p2 where the four octets directly represent the IPv4 address. The passive mode reply format 227 Entering Passive Mode (h1,h2,h3,h4,p1,p2) has the same assumption. HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2616) and URLs (RFC 1738) assume host fields can be dotted-decimal IPv4 addresses.

Email and messaging protocols reveal dependencies too. SMTP (RFC 2821) discussion of A and MX records, where IPv4 and IPv6 only nodes might cause failures. POP and IMAP URLs incorporate URL formats (like RFC 1738) that depend on IPv4 handling. iCalendar (RFC 2445) suggests using IP addresses as unique identifiers, assuming IPv4 format. Many protocols in service discovery (SLP, RFC 2608) and configuration (DHCP-derived fields in RFC 3017) explicitly embed IPv4 address formats.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP says "give me an address as four numbers and a port." URLs say "the host part might be four numbers with dots." DNS and email depend on IPv4 address records. All of these need to be updated or made flexible.

sections.title: Standards with No IPv4 Dependencies
sections.content:
A significant number of Application Area standards have no IPv4 dependencies. These include many of the basic Telnet options (RFCs 855–861), the Echo and Discard protocols (RFCs 862–863), TFTP (RFC 1350), SMTP service extensions (RFCs 1870, 2920, 2554), POP3 (RFC 1939), IMAP4 extensions (RFCs 2342, 2359, 2971), LDAP (RFC 2589), calendaring protocols (RFCs 2446–2447), media features, MIME types, and more modern formats like XML media types (RFC 3023).

This is good news: these standards already work with both IPv4 and IPv6 because they do not hardcode address formats or examples. Standards that reference hosts by name rather than by address literals, or that use abstract data types for network identifiers, proved to be future-proof.
sections.plainLanguage: Many rules don't mention addresses at all—they just say "send to the host" without caring what format the address is. Those don't need updating.

sections.title: Recommendations for Protocol Updates
sections.content:
The survey recommends that standards with IPv4 dependencies be updated or obsoleted by new versions that are address-independent. Where address literals are unavoidable, the RFC suggests following RFC 2732 format for literal IPv6 addresses (using square brackets, such as [2001:db8::1]). Protocols using URLs should ensure they reference RFC 2732 along with RFC 1738. Protocols that use IP addresses in examples should clarify they work with both IPv4 and IPv6.

Standards that explicitly limit or prefer IPv4 (such as FTP with its fixed four-octet format) require protocol redesign, not just clarification. The RFC emphasizes that the goal is either full address independence (preferred) or dual-stack IPv4 and IPv6 support (acceptable interim step).
sections.plainLanguage: Some rules can be fixed by adding a note "this works with any address format." Others need new versions of the protocol that work the same way for both old and new addresses.
